extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers studying Virginia state government and civics
extracted.subtask_description: Summary and explanation of constitutional powers, limits, offices, qualifications, and court structure under the Virginia Constitution. Focuses on what the General Assembly, Governor, judiciary, and local governments may or may not do and the procedural rules governing offices and courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of speech and press limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The General Assembly cannot pass a law abridging the freedom of speech or of the press.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individuals are granted the right to participate in political discussion and criticism and interchange ideas; not absolute — one cannot utter or publish untruths, incite insurrections, encourage disobedience of laws, defame the government, or give aid and comfort to foreign countries at war with the United States. The text notes the necessity for such limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eminent domain and just compensation
rubrics_metrics.description: The General Assembly cannot enact a law whereby private property would be taken or damaged for public uses without just compensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The General Assembly defines 'Public Uses' (legislative power); the sovereign power to take private property for public purposes with proper compensation is called 'right of eminent domain.' In disputes over fair value, the court decides the fair amount.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious freedom protections
rubrics_metrics.description: The General Assembly cannot compel an individual to frequent or support a particular religious place of worship, force suffering for religious beliefs, require religious tests, bestow privileges on a sect, or authorize an official church.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also cannot levy taxes forcing support of any particular church, cannot incorporate churches or grant charters of incorporation to any religious denomination — provisions echo Jefferson's 'Statute of Virginia for Religious Freedom.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on lotteries
rubrics_metrics.description: The General Assembly is forbidden to authorize lotteries or to allow residents to buy, sell, or transfer lottery tickets or chances.

rubrics_metrics.name: County creation and alteration rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The General Assembly has power to form, divide and consolidate counties, with specific size and population requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A new county must have minimum area of 600 square miles; the county or counties from which it is formed cannot be less than 600 square miles after formation; no county can be reduced in population below 8,000. Division may occur when a county's length is three times its breadth or exceeds fifty miles. Consolidation requires approval by a majority of qualified voters in each county in a special election.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical county changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Narration of original counties and subsequent changes (e.g., 98 counties now; last change in 1952 when Elizabeth City County and Warwick County became independent cities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains evolution of county numbers and that General Assembly will continue exercising county-making powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of legislative authority versus constitutional restraints
rubrics_metrics.description: The State constitution is usually considered a restraining instrument; the General Assembly has all powers not prohibited by State or Federal Constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotation: 'The authority of the General Assembly shall extend to all subjects of legislation, not herein forbidden or unrestricted...' and omission of specific grants should not be construed to deprive authority unless purpose plainly appears.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on local/special/private laws (enumerated instances)
rubrics_metrics.description: The General Assembly cannot enact any local, special or private law in specified instances (but may enact general laws on same subjects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enumerated instances include laws: (1) for the punishment of crime, (2) changing venue, (3) regulating jurisdiction or rules of evidence, (4) changing county seats, (5) assessing/collecting taxes or extending time for assessment/collection, (6) exempting property from taxation, (7) postponing/diminishing obligations to State/local unit, (8) refunding money lawfully paid into treasury, (9) granting extra compensation from treasury to officers/agents/contractors, (10) conducting elections or designating voting places, (11) regulating labor/trade/mining/manufacturing or interest rates, (12) granting any pension, (13) changing fees/salaries/allowances of public officers during term, (14) declaring streams navigable or authorizing construction/removal of obstructions, (15) regulating fencing or boundaries or running at large of stock, (16) creating private corporations or amending charters, (17) granting special/exclusive rights to private entities, (18) naming/changing name of private corporation, (19) forfeiting charter of a private corporation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment/repeal of general laws
rubrics_metrics.description: General laws pertaining to the above subjects may be amended or repealed provided they do not have the effect of enacting a special, private, or local law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delegation of local powers by general law
rubrics_metrics.description: The General Assembly, by general law, may confer upon county boards and city/town councils powers of local and special legislation as long as delegation is not inconsistent with constitutional limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Auditing committee duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Each regular legislature session appoints a standing auditing committee (2 Senate members, 3 House members) whose chief function is to examine books of State Treasurer and executive officers concerned with auditing/accounting at least once a year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This committee reports results to the Governor and must arrange publication in two newspapers of general circulation; may employ accountants; Governor submits such reports to the General Assembly at session start.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governor election timing and term
rubrics_metrics.description: Governor is elected by qualified voters on the Tuesday following the first Monday in November of every other odd-numbered year; term is four years; not eligible for re-election to the same office during the succeeding term (cannot succeed himself).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Term begins third Wednesday in January in year after election and ends on the Tuesday following the second Wednesday in January of his fourth year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governor qualifications
rubrics_metrics.description: To be eligible for Governor: (1) must be a United States citizen (if naturalized, naturalized at least ten years prior), (2) at least thirty years of age, (3) resident in Virginia for at least five years directly preceding election.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governor residency, salary, and emoluments restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Governor must live in Richmond during term, resides at Executive Mansion, receives salary (stated $20,000 at time of text) that cannot be increased or diminished during term; cannot receive any other emolument while in office from state or other government and cannot hold any other position while Governor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governor duties and enumerated powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Chief duty is to faithfully administer laws; enumerated powers include reporting condition of State (Governor's Message), recommending measures, convening General Assembly on request or special session, commander-in-chief of State forces, calling out militia/State Police, conducting relations with other states, suspending officers during recess (with reporting), appointing pro tempore successors during recess, filling pro tempore vacancies with commissions expiring automatically after thirty days of next session, remitting fines/penalties under law, granting reprieves and pardons (with exceptions), removing political disabilities, commuting capital sentences, reporting details of remissions/pardons/commutations and reasons, requiring information under oath from executive officers and inspecting books/accounts, requiring written opinions from Attorney-General, certifying commissions with official seal, supervising executive departments and appointing chief officers with General Assembly consent, appointing certain officials subject to confirmation (e.g., Secretary of Commonwealth, State Treasurer), considering all bills passed by General Assembly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many powers are qualified (e.g., suspensions and appointments during recess are temporary and require later reporting); appointment confirmations involve General Assembly consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governor legislative action options on bills
rubrics_metrics.description: After a bill passes both houses, the Governor may: (1) sign it into law; (2) veto it and return with objections (General Assembly may override veto by two-thirds of members present in each house; Governor has item veto power on appropriation bills); (3) do nothing — if General Assembly still in session after five days (Sundays excepted), bill becomes law; (4) do nothing — if General Assembly has adjourned within ten days, the bill does not become law (pocket veto).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When vetoed, returning house enters objections on journal and reconsiders; for amendments recommended by Governor, only a majority of members present in each house is required to amend. Item veto affects only designated items which then are reconsidered with same override procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lieutenant-Governor election, qualifications, duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Lieutenant-Governor is elected at same time as Governor for a four-year term with identical qualifications and election procedure; succeeds to Governorship if Governor dies, resigns, removed, fails to qualify or unable to discharge duties; chief duty is permanent chairman (President) of State Senate, no vote except in case of a tie.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Salary: $1260 per biennial session plus $3,000 per year travel expenses (same as Speaker of House of Delegates at time of text).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointment confirmation rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals appointed by the Governor to offices requiring General Assembly confirmation who do not receive confirmation cannot start or continue in office and are ineligible for reappointment during the recess of the General Assembly to fill a vacancy caused by such refused confirmation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary of the Commonwealth duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Secretary acts as official secretary to the Governor and head of Division of Records where all records of Governor's official acts are kept; custodian of the official State Seal and responsible for affixing it to official documents signed by Governor.

rubrics_metrics.name: State Treasurer duties
rubrics_metrics.description: State Treasurer has custody of state funds, pays bills, deposits revenue in specified banks, and withdraws money only upon the State Comptroller's warrant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Auditor of Public Accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Elected by joint vote of both houses for a four-year term; duties include auditing all accounts of each state department, institution and agency; chief auditor and accountant of the Auditing Committee; responsible for exposing unauthorized, illegal or unwise handling of state funds and required to audit city and county officials' accounts unless audited annually by a certified public accountant following State Auditor instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bond requirement for public funds officers
rubrics_metrics.description: All state officials who collect, keep, handle or disburse public funds must give bond for faithful performance of duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amount of bond varies with amount of revenue involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial Department structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Virginia provides a Supreme Court of Appeals, Circuit Courts, City Courts and other inferior courts; jurisdiction regulated by law except where the Constitution grants specific jurisdiction; General Assembly authorizes appointment of judges pro tempore by Governor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supreme Court of Appeals composition and qualifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Supreme Court of Appeals consists of seven members (one Chief Justice and six associate justices); Chief Justice is the Senior Justice by years of continuous service (ties broken by age); term of office twelve years; elected by joint vote of Senate and House of Delegates; constitutional qualification: must have held a 'judicial station' in the U.S. or have practiced law in Virginia or another state for five years prior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Salaries: justice $15,500; Chief Justice additional $4,500 (figures in text).

rubrics_metrics.name: Supreme Court division procedure and decision rules
rubrics_metrics.description: When meeting in session, the Court may sit as full court or in two divisions of not less than three justices each; each division has full power to determine causes, issue writs, and exercise powers; a division's decision does not become judgment of the full court unless concurred in by at least three judges; any case involving construction of State or U.S. Constitution must be decided by full court with assent of at least four judges; if division cannot resolve constitutional questions, case must be reheard by full court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If divisions differ or a judge certifies conflict with prior decision within time/manner fixed by rules, the cause must be considered by full court or a quorum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original vs appellate jurisdiction of Supreme Court
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two types of jurisdiction: original (right to hear a case first time) and appellate (hearing a case appealed). The Supreme Court of Appeals has original jurisdiction in cases of habeas corpus, mandamus and prohibition; in other cases it has appellate jurisdiction only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions: habeas corpus commands bringing detained person before court; mandamus is order to subordinate courts/corporations to do specified act; prohibition restrains someone from doing a particular action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circuit Courts: creation, composition and jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: General Assembly arranges judicial circuits; no new circuit can be created containing less than forty thousand inhabitants (by latest census) nor if creation reduces existing circuits below forty thousand; there are thirty-seven judicial circuits; each circuit has one judge chosen by joint vote of both houses for eight-year term; must have same qualifications as Supreme Court justices and live in circuit while in office; circuit courts have original and appellate jurisdiction in (1) all civil cases involving twenty dollars or more and (2) certain criminal cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: City (Corporation/Hustings) Courts
rubrics_metrics.description: City Hustings or Corporation Courts are courts of record with original jurisdiction except appeals from justices; they can try felonies committed within one mile of corporation limits; there are specific city courts listed; judges must live in the city where court is located (with some exceptions for small cities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: City court judges chosen for eight-year term by joint vote; in cities with less than ten thousand inhabitants, a corporation court judge may live outside city limits and may serve as judge of another small city.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of cities for court purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: Cities are divided into two classes: (1) first class — population at least ten thousand by last official census; (2) second class — population less than ten thousand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In each first class city there may be a corporation court in addition to circuit court. In any city containing at least thirty thousand inhabitants, the General Assembly may provide additional courts and judges as deemed necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abolishment of city courts procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: A city court may be abolished by a majority vote of qualified voters in the city at a special election held for that purpose, or automatically if the office of judge with annual salary less than eight hundred dollars becomes vacant and remains vacant for ninety consecutive days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Upon abolishment, the city immediately comes within the jurisdiction of the circuit court of the county in which it is situated; records transfer accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judges: commission, salary protection, vacancies and removal
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges are commissioned by the Governor; salaries and allowances prescribed by law cannot be diminished during term; term begins Feb 1 after election; successor elected for unexpired term when vacancy; General Assembly may retire judges and provide duties to retired judges; salaries are paid from State treasury but State reimbursed for one-half of circuit judges' salaries by counties/cities (with exceptions); judges may be removed for cause by concurrent vote of both houses with cause entered on journal and judge given at least twenty days' notice with copy of alleged causes; typically judges cannot practice law or hold other public office while in office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formality of writs and indictments
rubrics_metrics.description: Writs must be issued in the name of the 'Commonwealth of Virginia' and certified by clerks; indictments must conclude 'against the peace and dignity of the Commonwealth.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Lower courts, magistrates and specialized courts
rubrics_metrics.description: General Assembly provides for appointment/election of justices of the peace and establishes their jurisdiction; Virginia has police justices, trial justices, civil and police justices, juvenile and domestic relations courts and mayor's courts with limited jurisdiction; magistrate courts/justice of the peace courts handle misdemeanors and small civil cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special courts: two Law and Chancery Courts (Roanoke, Norfolk) for probate/estates; special Chancery Court in Richmond for wills north of James River; special Law and Equity Court in Richmond; Juvenile and Domestic Relations Court in Norfolk has jurisdiction over dependent/neglected/delinquent children and family-related crimes except manslaughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: State Attorney-General election and duties
rubrics_metrics.description: State Attorney-General is elected by qualified voters at same time and term as Governor and Lieutenant-Governor (four-year term); must have same qualifications as Governor but eligible for re-election; chief duty is attorney-at-law for the State: renders opinions on interpretation/application of laws upon request, presents State interest cases to Supreme Court of Appeals, represents Virginia before the U.S. Supreme Court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Has legal assistants to aid local Commonwealth attorneys; subject to removal in same manner as judges; salary stated as $17,000 annually in text.
